name: Rhizoctonia sore shin / root and crown rot
summary: A soilborne Cannabis root, crown, and lower-stem disease in which dry brown root rot or reddish-brown lower-stem rot can accompany wilt. The canopy response and lesion color overlap multiple root-zone problems, so image or video evidence alone supports only a low-confidence Rhizoctonia-compatible label.
affectedParts: lower main stem at and just above the soil line
leaves and buds when directly infected
indicators: Dry brown rot is visible on plant-linked Cannabis roots
Reddish-brown rot develops on the lower main stem at or near the soil line
A necrotic lesion just above the soil line accompanies wilt on the same plant
Root and crown necrosis is documented with intact root-to-stem continuity rather than an unlinked close-up
Dry brown leaf tissue or bud infection can occur, but these above-ground lesions are not sufficient for a Rhizoctonia label
Pigmented septate hyphae recovered from an active lesion branch at roughly 90 degrees with basal constriction
Validated sequence or other qualified laboratory evidence supports Rhizoctonia solani from the same plant and lesion
A whole-plant view, soil-line view, and washed-root view show the spatial relationship and progression of compatible disease
exclusions: White cottony basal mycelium with numerous round tan-to-brown sclerotia supports southern blight instead
Soft, water-soaked or sloughed roots plus oomycete evidence support Pythium or another water mold
Vascular discoloration and plant-linked Fusarium isolation or molecular evidence support Fusarium crown/root disease
Black root or crown tissue with microsclerotia and Macrophomina evidence supports charcoal rot
Firm integrated root galls plus nematode recovery support root-knot nematodes
Circling or matted roots follow the container wall and no active necrotic lesion or pathogen evidence is present, supporting root binding
No basal or root lesion is found and measured moisture, oxygen, EC, pH, or water-status data explain the canopy response
A detached root, stem lesion, or canopy image cannot be linked to the sampled plant and laboratory result

progression.description: The disease is historically documented in Cannabis seedlings, but a symptom-free image cannot establish infection and seedling onset is not universal.
Dry brown rot becomes visible on roots; record lesion margins and distribution across the intact washed root system.
Reddish-brown rot or a necrotic lesion develops on the lower main stem at or just above the soil line.
Compatible necrosis extends through plant-linked roots, crown, or lower stem while root function declines.
Wilt, reduced vigor, or collapse may become evident, but no source establishes a diagnostic leaf-age, canopy-position, or temporal pattern.

confirmation: Capture the same plant at whole-canopy, soil-line, crown, and washed-root scales with a ruler or other scale and preserve intact root-to-stem continuity.
Sample several fresh active lesion margins from the lower stem, crown, and roots under one plant identifier; retain paired apparently healthy tissue and substrate history.

Examine lesion-derived fungal growth microscopically for pigmented septate hyphae, approximately right-angle branching, and basal constriction; morphology supports a differential but is not sufficient ground truth by itself.
Use a qualified plant-diagnostic laboratory and validated molecular identification from the plant-linked lesion when assigning Rhizoctonia solani.
Investigate Pythium or other oomycetes, Fusarium, southern blight, charcoal rot, and nematodes when signs are mixed or the first assay is negative.
Measure root-zone moisture, oxygen or drainage, EC, pH, temperature, container geometry, and irrigation history so abiotic stress and disease-conducive context are separated from organism identity.

Keep canopy-only, root-only, detached, morphology-only, ITS-only, mixed-pathogen, unlinked-laboratory, low-resolution, stock, forum, vendor, or generated samples out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Separate suspect root-zone material and prevent movement of potentially contaminated soil, roots, debris, containers, runoff, or tools into clean areas.
Preserve fresh plant-linked lesion margins for diagnostic testing before destructive treatment or disposal.
Check drainage, irrigation, EC, pH, oxygenation, and container restriction concurrently without treating any one condition as proof of Rhizoctonia.
correctivePlan: Base disease-specific action on a qualified diagnosis and locally appropriate crop rules; this profile does not convert symptom appearance or warm-soil context into a treatment decision.
Correct measured root-zone stressors and track response with repeated linked canopy, soil-line, and root observations; visual improvement does not prove pathogen elimination.
prevention: Use clean propagation material, media, containers, and tools and avoid moving infected plant debris or soil between production areas.
Inspect transplants at the soil line and roots before placement while retaining plant and source-lot identifiers.
Record irrigation and soil-temperature history because early over-irrigation and cooler emergence conditions can increase risk without proving disease.
warnings: Wilt, reduced vigor, brown roots, and reddish-brown stem lesions are not organism-specific.
The Cannabis-specific compendium statement is historical seedling-disease evidence from Ukraine; it does not establish current prevalence or a universal stage of onset.
The Pacific Northwest environment and symptom descriptions are crop-specific but do not establish a universal cultivar response, severity scale, or image-only label.
Rhizoctonia can coexist with other root pathogens, nematodes, container restriction, or abiotic stress, and a single assay or image may not resolve a mixed case.
Photo/video-only confidence is capped at 0.20; confirmed labels require plant-linked diagnostic evidence and human review.

The USDA Hemp Multistate Project S1084 Kentucky image is a whole-field institutional reference without visible root, crown, lower-stem, lesion, scale, specimen identifier, laboratory linkage, or item-level reuse license; it is hidden, metadata-only, and training-ineligible.

sources.title: Surveying for Potential Diseases and Abiotic Disorders of Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Production
supportedClaims: A North Carolina 2017–2018 hemp diagnostic survey identified 16 diseases caused by fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes; the study used clinic diagnostics, morphology, sequence data for representative organisms, and pathogenicity testing for its confirmed disease set.

Fusarium foliar and flower blight was common in submitted samples and involved F. equiseti and F. graminearum; flowers developed surface hyphae and light-brown necrotic tips while leaves developed circular light-brown lesions about 1 cm wide with dark margins and gray-brown aging centers.
Exserohilum rostratum leaf spot occurred on leaves and stems as round brown-to-black lesions with darkened margins and abundant conidia, with ITS1/RPB2 evidence supporting the identification.

Rhizoctonia solani was found on roots and crowns with plant wilting and necrotic lesions just above the soil line; pigmented septate hyphae showed characteristic right-angle branching and sequence evidence supported R. solani.

Southern blight caused whole-plant wilt in reproductive hemp during hot midseason conditions, with abundant hyphae and russet-brown sclerotia on roots/lower stems and sequence/phylogenetic evidence supporting Athelia rolfsii/Sclerotium rolfsii.
Meloidogyne incognita was identified from galled hemp roots with females and egg masses; affected plants had some associated stunting.

The survey documented Serratia-associated, vein-limited angular hemp lesions and red bacterial ooze emerging from punctured lesions, while emphasizing that hemp leaf diseases overlap visually and require diagnostic separation.

sources.title: Rhizoctonia Sore Shin and Root Rot
supportedClaims: The Cannabis-specific compendium identifies sore shin and root rot as a disease caused by the soil fungus Rhizoctonia solani.

The chapter describes Rhizoctonia sore shin and root rot as the first recorded seedling disease of Cannabis in Ukraine; this is historical crop evidence and does not establish current prevalence, cultivar response, or a universal seedling-onset rule.

The chapter is Cannabis-specific and peer reviewed, but the abstract alone does not support assigning Rhizoctonia from canopy wilt, lesion color, production environment, or an image without organism-linked evidence.

sources.organization: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
authors: Pacific Northwest Plant Disease Management Handbook
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho
supportedClaims: The March 2026 institutional revision identifies Rhizoctonia solani as the cause, states that it can persist in soil for at least several years, has a broad host range, and can spread with infected plant debris.
The hemp description records dry brown root rot and reddish-brown rot on the lower main stem; it also reports dry brown leaf tissue and bud infection in Oregon medical Cannabis.

Warmer soil favors disease, while early over-irrigation and irrigation-related soil cooling can slow emergence and favor the fungus; these conditions are epidemiologic context and are not diagnostic proof.

The handbook recommends rotation away from susceptible hosts and avoiding early over-irrigation, supporting soil/debris movement and irrigation-history checks without establishing a universal treatment interval for every production system.

sources.title: Rhizoctonia Sore Shin and Root Rot
sources.publisher: Cornell University, University of Kentucky, and USDA Hemp Multistate Project S1084
supportedClaims: The institutional hemp-disease gallery categorizes eight Kentucky Cannabis/hemp photographs under Rhizoctonia sore shin and root rot, identifies Rhizoctonia solani, and credits the photographs to N. Gauthier.
The indexed 1920 by 1280 field photograph provides a whole-plot view of widespread late-season brown, dried, or collapsed plants rather than a root, crown, lower-stem, lesion, or microscopy view.

The gallery does not publish a plant identifier, cultivar, date, scale, severity rubric, sample-to-assay linkage, culture, sequence accession, pathogenicity result, or item-level diagnostic method for the pictured field; it therefore supports institutional reference context but not specimen-level Rhizoctonia ground truth.

The gallery page and asset metadata do not state an item-level reuse license or automated-training permission, so the photograph is retained as reference-link metadata only and is not displayed, copied into the repository, or admitted to training.
